arith.title: Multiplication
arith.intro: Multiplication is super-charged addition: 4 × 6 means 4 groups of 6. Learn the times tables and huge calculations become tiny.

steps.title: Groups of things
steps.body: 3 × 5 = 3 groups of 5 = 5+5+5 = 15. Picture rows of dots — 3 rows, 5 in each.

steps.title: Order never matters
steps.body: 4×7 = 7×4. If one direction is hard, flip it! Learning tables is half the work.

steps.title: Break big ones apart
steps.body: Split a hard multiplication into easy pieces and add: 6×12 = 6×10 + 6×2.

steps.title: Multiplying by 10, 100
steps.body: Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place left — it does NOT just “add a zero” to decimals!

mistakes: Guessing tables you have not learned — practice beats guessing.
Adding instead of multiplying when reading word problems.
“Adding a zero” for ×10 on decimals (3.5 → 3.50 is wrong; it is 35).

glossary.meaning: the answer to a multiplication
the multiplication facts up to 12×12

frac.title: Fractions
frac.intro: A fraction is a way to talk about parts of a whole thing. If you cut a pizza into 4 equal slices and take 1, you have 1/4 — one out of four parts.

steps.title: Meet the two numbers
steps.body: The TOP number (numerator) counts how many parts you have. The BOTTOM number (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole was cut into.
steps.example: 3/4 → you have 3 parts, the whole was cut into 4.

steps.title: Equal parts matter
steps.body: Fractions only work when every part is the same size. Half a pizza means the pizza was cut into 2 EQUAL pieces.

steps.title: Same value, different look
steps.body: Multiply or divide the top AND bottom by the same number and the fraction keeps the same value. That is how you simplify.

steps.title: Adding with the same bottom
steps.body: If the denominators match, just add the tops and keep the bottom.

steps.title: Adding with different bottoms
steps.body: First rewrite both fractions with a common denominator, then add the tops.

examples.solution:
Divide top and bottom by 2.
6÷2 = 3, 8÷2 = 4.
Answer: 3/4.

Make the bottoms match: 15.
2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15.
10 > 9, so 2/3 is bigger.

mistakes: Adding the bottoms too: 1/4 + 1/4 is 2/4, NOT 2/8!
Forgetting parts must be EQUAL — 3 unequal slices are not thirds.
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction — 1/8 is smaller than 1/4.

glossary.meaning: top number — parts you have
bottom number — equal parts in the whole
different-looking fractions with the same value
divide top and bottom until the numbers are as small as possible

dec.title: Percentages
dec.intro: A percentage is a special fraction that is always out of 100. “50%” just means 50 out of every 100 — which is one half.

steps.title: Percent = out of 100
steps.body: The word comes from “per centum” — for each hundred. So 25% is 25 out of 100, the same as 25/100 or 1/4.

steps.title: Find easy percentages first
steps.body: 10% means divide by 10. 50% means divide by 2. 25% means divide by 4. Most percentages can be built from these!

steps.title: The general trick
steps.body: To find p% of a number: multiply the number by p, then divide by 100.

steps.title: Switching forms
steps.body: Fraction → percent: divide top by bottom, times 100. Decimal → percent: times 100.

examples.problem: A $40 shirt is 25% off. New price?

mistakes: Thinking 5% is the same as 0.5 — it is actually 0.05.
“50% more” is not the same as “50% of” — more means you ADD it on.
Percentages over 100% are fine — 200% of 5 is 10.

glossary.meaning: out of every 100
an amount taken OFF a price
how much something grew or shrank, out of 100

neg.title: Negative Numbers
neg.intro: Negative numbers are the numbers below zero — like a freezer at −5° or a submarine 20 meters below the surface. They sit to the LEFT of 0 on the number line.

steps.title: Picture the number line
steps.body: Zero in the middle, positives to the right, negatives to the left. Moving right = adding, moving left = subtracting.

steps.title: Adding a negative = subtracting
steps.body: Adding −4 is the same as subtracting 4. Two signs together squish into one.

steps.title: Subtracting a negative = adding
steps.body: Taking away a debt makes you richer! Minus a minus turns into plus.

steps.title: Multiplying and dividing
steps.body: Same signs → positive answer. Different signs → negative answer.

examples.problem: The temperature is 3° and falls 8°. What now?

mistakes: Thinking −9 is bigger than −2 — it is SMALLER (further left).
Forgetting that minus a minus is a plus.
Losing the sign when multiplying: count the negative signs!

glossary.meaning: a number less than zero
a line of numbers — negatives left, positives right
same distance from 0, other side: 4 and −4

ops.title: Order of Operations
ops.intro: When a calculation has several operations, math has traffic rules about what to do first. Brackets, then powers, then multiply/divide, then add/subtract — that is why 2 + 3 × 4 is 14, not 20.

steps.title: Learn the order
steps.body: B-O-DMAS / P-E-MDAS: Brackets first, then pOwers (exponents), then Multiply & Divide (left to right), finally Add & Subtract (left to right).

steps.title: Multiply/divide are EQUAL partners
steps.body: They have the same priority — when both appear, just go left to right. Same for add/subtract.

steps.title: Brackets are your tool
steps.body: Want the addition to happen first? Wrap it in brackets. Brackets beat everything.

mistakes: Always going left to right and ignoring the rules.
Doing addition before multiplication because it “comes first” in the line.
Treating multiplication as stronger than division — they are equal, go left to right.

glossary.meaning: memory trick for the order: brackets, powers, ×÷, +−
the ( ) that force a part to be done first

alg.title: Solving Equations
alg.intro: An equation is like a perfectly balanced scale: whatever is on the left weighs exactly the same as what is on the right. Solving it means finding the mystery number (usually called x) that keeps it balanced.

steps.title: The golden rule
steps.body: Whatever you do to one side, do EXACTLY the same to the other side. Add 3 on the left? Add 3 on the right. That keeps the scale balanced.
steps.example: x − 3 = 7 → add 3 to BOTH sides → x = 10.

steps.title: Undo things in reverse
steps.body: To free x, peel operations away using opposites: + undoes −, × undoes ÷. Do it one step at a time.

steps.title: Check your answer
steps.body: Put your x back into the original equation. If both sides match, you nailed it.

examples.solution:
x is being divided by 4,
so multiply both sides by 4:
x = 24.

mistakes: Doing something to only ONE side of the equation.
Forgetting to flip the operation: to undo +5 you must SUBTRACT 5.
Skipping the check at the end — it takes 5 seconds and catches everything.

glossary.meaning: a math sentence with an equals sign
the mystery letter (like x) standing for a number
find the value that makes both sides equal

geo.title: Area & Perimeter
geo.intro: Perimeter is the distance all the way AROUND a shape — like a fence. Area is the amount of surface INSIDE it — like the grass. They answer different questions!

steps.title: Perimeter = add the sides
steps.body: Walk around the shape and add every side length. For a rectangle: 2×(width + height).

steps.title: Area of a rectangle
steps.body: Count the unit squares that fit inside — that is width × height. Area is measured in SQUARE units like cm².

steps.title: Area of a triangle
steps.body: A triangle is half of a rectangle. Area = base × height ÷ 2.

steps.title: Weird shapes? Split them!
steps.body: Cut an L-shape into rectangles, find each area, and add them up.

examples.problem: A garden is 8 m by 5 m. How much fence and how much grass?
Triangle: base 10 cm, height 6 cm. Area?

mistakes: Mixing them up — fence problems are perimeter, paint/carpet problems are area.
Forgetting the ÷2 for triangles.
Writing area in cm instead of cm².

glossary.meaning: distance around the outside
surface inside, in square units
the two measurements you multiply for triangles

pow.title: Exponents (Powers)
pow.intro: An exponent is a shortcut for repeated multiplication. Instead of writing 2×2×2 you write 2³ — “2 to the power of 3”. The little number counts how many copies get multiplied.

steps.title: Base and exponent
steps.body: In 5³, the 5 is the base (what you multiply) and 3 is the exponent (how many copies).

steps.title: Squares and cubes
steps.body: Power 2 is called “squared” (area of a square!), power 3 is “cubed” (volume of a cube!).

steps.title: It is NOT multiplying by the exponent
steps.body: The most common trap: 2⁴ is 2×2×2×2 = 16, not 2×4 = 8.

steps.title: Powers of 10
steps.body: 10ⁿ is a 1 followed by n zeros. That is how scientists write huge numbers.

mistakes: Multiplying base × exponent (2³ is 8, not 6!).
Forgetting x⁰ = 1.
Mixing up 2³ and 3² — order matters.

glossary.meaning: the number being multiplied
the little number counting the copies
to the power of 2

stat.title: Mean, Median & Mode
stat.intro: These are three different ways to describe the “middle” of a bunch of numbers. Mean = share equally, median = the middle one, mode = the most common one.

steps.title: Mean — the equal share
steps.body: Add all the numbers, then divide by how many numbers there are. It is what people usually call the average.

steps.title: Median — the middle
steps.body: Sort the numbers, then pick the one exactly in the middle. With an even count, take the mean of the middle two.

steps.title: Mode — the popular one
steps.body: The value that appears most often. There can be one mode, several, or none.

steps.title: Range — the spread
steps.body: Biggest minus smallest. It tells you how spread out the numbers are.

examples.problem: Test scores: 6, 9, 9, 4. Find mean, median, mode.

mistakes: Forgetting to SORT before finding the median.
Dividing by the wrong count for the mean.
Saying the mode is how many times it appears — it is the VALUE itself.

glossary.meaning: add all ÷ count — the equal share
middle value after sorting
most frequent value
biggest minus smallest
